texts: Graphene Failure
The predicted failure mode depends on the tensile state.
Paper

Failure Mechanisms of
Graphene under Tension
Authors and journal

C. A. Marianetti & H. G.
Yevick · Physical Review
Letters 105 (2010)

Fig. 4(a). Maximum stable strain across tensile directions; regions differ in which
instability occurs first.
What limits near-ideal graphene?
The first failure mechanism under a generic tensile state was still an open question.
The prior experiment and calculations probe different loading contexts.
Nanoindentation

Lee et al. strained graphene to failure under
conditions described as nearly ideal.
Uniaxial phonons

Earlier calculations found elastic instability
for armchair or zigzag loading.
Open question

Which instability occurs first for a generic
state of tension?
This study

Compare the elastic limit with a finite-wave-
vector K1 phonon instability.
How are both limits tested?
The workflow compares elastic instability with the K1-mode onset.
1 · Strain states

Evaluate strain-dependent tensile response,
including equibiaxial loading.
2 · DFT forces

Generate strained-structure forces using the
local density approximation.
3 · Phonons

Calculate phonons with the displacement
method.
4 · Compare limits

Track the elastic instability against the K1-
mode onset.
When does the K1 mode soften?
Two calculations place K1 softening near ε_A ≈ 0.21.
These are calculated thresholds for idealized equibiaxial loading, not measured breaking strains.
Phonon threshold

K1 softens at ε_A = 0.205–0.212 under
equibiaxial strain.
Independent check

Mode-energy analysis predicts ε_A = 0.213,
closely matching the phonon threshold.

Fig. 1. In-plane phonon branches under equibiaxial strain;
the K1 mode approaches instability at K.
How can K1 softening reduce strength?

The authors link K1 softening to a structural transition and reduced strength in some tensile
states.
Structural route

The authors infer that the deepening K1 double well
leads toward isolated hexagonal rings.
Strength implication

The K-cell stress drops near softening; the
proposed route can reduce strength.

Fig. 3. Nominal stress versus equibiaxial strain; the
K-cell response drops near K1 softening.
Tensile state selects the failure mode
Elastic instability governs regions I and III; the K1 mode occurs first in region II.
Regions I and III
Elastic instability precedes the K1 mode.
Region II

The K1-mode instability arrives first; the
route changes with tensile direction.

Fig. 4(a). Maximum stable strain across tensile directions; regions I/
III are elastic-limited and region II is K1-limited.
Do orientation and shear matter?

Rotation and shear make only small changes to the predicted K1 onset, but the state map is
incomplete.
Rotation and shear checks do not enumerate every possible tensile state.
Rotation

The 15° map stays within the original/rotated
envelope; orientations were sampled every 3°.
Shear and scope

Shear shifts K1 onset only slightly. Anisotropy
leaves some tensile states untested.

Fig. 4(c). At 15° rotation, the failure map remains
within the original/rotated envelope.
Experiment vs prediction?

The measured nominal strain (0.225) is closer to the calculated elastic limit (0.216), but the
failure route remains unresolved.
K1 stabilization is a proposed explanation, not a demonstrated mechanism.
Measured

Nanoindentation reports nominal
equibiaxial breaking strain 0.225.
Calculated elastic limit
The equibiaxial elastic-instability strain is 0.216.
Authors’ proposal

The K1 mode may be stabilized
during nanoindentation.
Possible differences

Indenter environment and strain construction may
affect the comparison.
Conclusions and limits
Tensile state selects whether elastic instability or a K1 soft mode limits strength.
PaperWorkflow evidence coverage is under review; the paper also notes that rotation/shear sampling is not exhaustive.
Mode selection

Elastic failure in regions I/III; K1 soft-
mode failure in region II.
Open limits

Indentation leaves the route unresolved;
rotation/shear sampling is incomplete.

Fig. 4(a). The loading-direction map summarizes where elastic and
K1-mode instabilities occur first.
